sources.news_title: Judge Tosses Hunter Biden Laptop Perjury Case Against Ex-FBI
sources.text:
A federal magistrate judge in Washington on Monday threw out the Justice Department's criminal case against two former senior FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about the bureau's handling of Hunter Biden's laptop, finding no probable cause for the charges and describing the prosecution, brought two weeks before the midterm elections, as something that "cannot be described as anything other than weaponization." The ruling by U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, delivered from the bench after a three-day evidentiary hearing, is the latest in a string of politically charged cases brought by the department this autumn to collapse before trial, and the first to fail on the government's own evidence rather than on the legitimacy of the prosecutor who filed it.
The complaint, filed October 20, accused Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, both former high-ranking officials in the FBI's Foreign Influence Task Force, of falsely downplaying to the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 their knowledge of and involvement in the bureau's investigations connected to the laptop that the department says Hunter Biden left at a Delaware repair shop in 2019. Prosecutors cited internal documents and witness accounts that they said showed the two regularly discussed the matter within the task force, and noted a 2020 "defensive briefing" the officials had given Republican senators. Faruqui found the case rested on assumptions rather than evidence: the government had presented no direct evidence of motive, he said, had not shown that either official knowingly made a false statement, and had not established that any statement was material to the committee's inquiry.
The hearing that produced the ruling was unusual in both its timing and its content. At a preliminary session last week Faruqui criticized prosecutors for filing an amended complaint with an additional charge overnight, directly to the docket, without first clearing it with the court, a maneuver he said he had never seen; he declined to approve an obstruction charge the department sought to add. An FBI agent who worked the case then testified that the investigation had been opened within hours of a speech President Donald Trump gave on election security last July, that it had been mandated by FBI Director Kash Patel, who kept close watch on it, and that the agent himself had been concerned it would be perceived as "political." Faruqui said Monday he was "deeply troubled" by the "critical mistakes" and the rushed nature of the case, and by its timing in the days before Tuesday's vote.
Dismissal of a complaint at this stage is not an acquittal. The department can still ask a grand jury to indict Floris and Benavides, or appeal Faruqui's ruling to the district's chief judge. But the department's record before Washington grand juries this year is the reason the path is not straightforward: on several occasions, grand jurors in the capital have refused to return indictments in high-profile cases the administration wanted brought. A federal judge separately dismissed the department's prosecutions of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James last year after finding that the prosecutor who filed them, Lindsey Halligan, had been unlawfully appointed. Lawyers for the two former officials said Monday the government "should heed the judge's decision and drop this case immediately."
The ruling arrives on the eve of an election in which the department's conduct has itself become an issue. In the past week federal judges have blocked the department from threatening election workers with prosecution, dismissed its suit to hold certification of Alaska's Senate race, and refused, in four separate courts, to let it segregate 20,000 California ballots; on Monday the administration took the last of those to the Supreme Court. The Floris and Benavides case was different in kind, a criminal prosecution rather than an election-administration suit, but Faruqui placed it in the same frame when he faulted the department for rushing to charge before the midterms, and the agent's testimony about how the case began gave that criticism a factual basis the other courts had not had.
For the two defendants, the practical effect is that they are, for now, not charged with anything. For the department, the effect is a judicial finding, on the record, that a case it chose to bring was political, made by a judge who heard its own agent say so. Whether it returns to a grand jury, and whether a grand jury agrees, will be an early test of how the department reads Tuesday's results.

Trump Suffers Major Legal Blow as Judge Tosses Case Against Two FBI Agents Accused of Hunter Biden Laptop 'Cover-Up'
Nov. 2 2026, Published 5:31 p.m. ET
President Donald Trump suffered a major legal loss as U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui dismissed criminal complaints on November 1 against two former senior FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about their knowledge of the investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop.
The judge cited what he called the “weaponization” of the Justice Department in his decision, RadarOnline can report.
Dismissed 'Weaponization' Criminal Complaints
Judge Faruqui dismissed the cases against Nikki Floris, 46, and Bradley Benavides, 56, after an hourlong ruling from the bench.
He said the investigation was rushed, conducted at the behest of Trump and FBI Director Kash Patel, and marred by “critical mistakes.”
Faruqui stated, “I am deeply troubled by what has happened here in this case. What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization.”
Prosecutors allegedly failed to establish that the former officials intentionally made false statements during their 2023 congressional testimony, that the statements affected the investigation, or that either official had a motive to deceive lawmakers.
“Without motive, without direct evidence, I have nothing,” Faruqui said regarding probable cause.
He described the government’s case as a “slapdash” effort and questioned why charges were brought in 2026 over testimony given three years earlier, just 10 days before the November 3 midterms.
“I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend that I cannot read a calendar,” he said.
How the Case Was Handled
Prosecutors charged Floris and Benavides through criminal complaints rather than seeking a grand jury indictment.
Faruqui questioned the decision, saying, “It is self-evident that the U.S. attorney’s office is avoiding taking this case to a grand jury.”
He also criticized an attempt to file an amended public complaint overnight with an additional obstruction charge without prior court approval, calling the overall process “a little sideshow on top of a little sideshow.”
However, the dismissal does not permanently end the case.
The Justice Department can still seek a grand jury indictment, though the department has struggled to obtain indictments in politically charged cases in Washington, D.C.
FBI Agent’s Testimony
During a three-day preliminary hearing the previous week, FBI agent Bryan Witt, who was assigned to the investigation, testified that colleagues viewed the inquiry as a “witch hunt” and that he personally considered it a “huge distraction” from his regular work.
Witt said the investigation began one day after Trump delivered a primetime election security speech revisiting his 2020 election grievances.
He also testified that Patel demanded and received constant updates, an unusual level of involvement.
Faruqui cited the pressure to deliver results quickly as a factor that led to critical mistakes, including the complaint incorrectly claiming the officials had provided sworn testimony when they were not under oath.
What the Officials Were Accused Of
Floris and Benavides were former leaders of the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force. Prosecutors alleged they falsely downplayed their knowledge of the Hunter Biden laptop investigation during 2023 House testimony.
Floris said she did not have details about the probe; Benavides said he learned about the laptop from a Wikipedia page shortly before testifying.
The judge ultimately found no plausible motive for either to intentionally mislead Congress.
Defense attorneys for Floris called the prosecution a “politically motivated smear campaign aimed at scoring political points before the midterm elections” and said the charges “should never have been brought in the first place.”

sources.news_title: Judge Dismisses Hunter Biden Laptop Case Against FBI Officials
sources.text:
A Washington magistrate judge dismissed charges Monday against two former FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden’s laptop, calling the Justice Department case pure weaponization.
Judge Zia Faruqui tossed the case after a two-day probable cause hearing last week and said the prosecution “cannot be described as anything other than weaponization” of the Justice Department. The targets were Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, both formerly of the FBI’s now-defunct Foreign Influence Task Force.
New York Post reporting described how Faruqui weighed each of the pair’s 10 alleged lies from their 2023 House Judiciary Committee interviews. Prosecutors needed only one falsehood per defendant to keep the case alive. They got none.
The Department of Justice pushed back hard. In a statement on X, DOJ said it “disagrees with the Magistrate’s decision, which remarkably appears to suggest that high-ranking government officials are immune from accountability for making materially false statements to Congress.” Officials added they are “evaluating all options” while claiming their actions remain guided by “the facts, the evidence, and the law, not politics.”
Floris’ legal team, led by Margaret Donovan, did not mince words after the ruling. The case was “nothing more than a politically-motivated smear campaign aimed at scoring political points before the midterm elections,” the team said Monday. The charges “should never have been brought in the first place.”
"nothing more than a politically-motivated smear campaign aimed at scoring political points before the midterm elections"
Floris had told the committee “I did not” when asked whether she had been involved in the Hunter Biden investigation. Prosecutors claimed otherwise. FBI Special Agent Bryan Witt, the government’s only witness, testified that agents reviewed “hundreds of thousands” of her internal communications “line by line.”
Witt’s explanation for the charge was blunt.
"The reason we charged her is because we know she was involved in the Baltimore investigation. She became involved by talking to the criminal division."
The Baltimore field office led the probe of Hunter Biden for tax fraud and gun crimes. Defense lawyers argued the events in question had happened three years before the committee appearance and that Floris supervised hundreds of employees in a high-demand counterintelligence role.
Donovan spent much of the second hearing day, a Wednesday, painting her client as an overworked bureaucrat. She pressed Witt on whether he accounted for the crushing hours of Floris’ job.
"How many hours [do you estimate she worked] in a day? Twelve, 14, 16? You didn’t factor in the demands of her position?"
Witt answered that he “didn’t see the relevance.” Donovan also attacked the government’s method, saying it was unfair to “cherry-pick... five or six conversations out of hundreds of thousands.”
Benavides faced similar accusations that he downplayed what he knew, including a claim he told the committee he learned particulars on Wikipedia. His lawyer, Ron Safer, argued the officials could have misspoken without lying. Safer noted that basic civics requires members of both parties on every committee and that government exhibits listed Democratic staffers by title.
When Witt admitted he should have said “I don’t know” about committee partisanship, Safer pressed him:
"But you didn’t. Should we infer that you knowingly and willingly violated your oath?"
Witt said no one had explained “the partisanship nature of the committee” to him. He also acknowledged FBI Director Kash Patel pressed for “check-ins” on the case “weekly.”
The hearing opened with another loss for prosecutors. Faruqui tossed a superseding complaint they filed after midnight. Fox News reported that the unsigned filing added felony obstruction charges without judicial approval and softened the description of the officials’ roles from being at the “center” of activities to merely “involved in” them.
Faruqui did not hide his irritation at the maneuver. He said the government “should have filed nothing,” called the filing “inappropriate,” and said it “harms the defendant.” He asked why prosecutors had “changed the entire history of how you charge cases” on this one matter and said it made it look “like the United States is afraid of me trying to find probable cause.”
During a break on the first day, Floris was seen weeping in the courthouse hallway. By Monday, the entire case was gone.
The New York Post broke the Hunter Biden laptop story in October 2020. Fifty-one former intelligence officials quickly suggested the report was Russian disinformation. An FBI agent later confirmed the laptop was Hunter Biden’s at his 2024 gun trial.
Floris and Benavides sat for Judiciary Committee interviews in 2023 as Congress examined how the bureau handled the laptop and related probes. Prosecutors later accused them of material false statements. Faruqui’s ruling stopped that effort cold and labeled it weaponization.
DOJ insists high-ranking officials are not immune from accountability for false statements to Congress. The magistrate judge looked at the evidence the government actually brought, the rushed superseding complaint, the single witness, and the selective message pulls, and shut the case down.
When a federal judge calls a Justice Department prosecution weaponization and throws out every alleged lie, the public gets a clear look at how political cases get built, and how they fall apart under oath.

sources.news_title: ‘Weaponization’: Judge blasts DOJ in dismissing case against ex-FBI agents who investigated Hunter Biden
sources.text:
A federal judge on Monday dismissed a false statements case against two former senior FBI agents accused of lying to Congress about past investigations of Hunter Biden.
In dismissing the case, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui delivered a scathing rebuke from the bench of current FBI and DOJ leadership, who he accused of seeking to impact the midterm elections.
“What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization,” the judge said in tossing the case against former FBI officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides.
The dismissal follows days of testimony in a series of rare public hearings Faruqui convened to determine whether the government’s case against Floris and Benavides met the low bar of probable cause.
Testimony from an FBI agent who led the case revealed it was initiated only after President Donald Trump held a July address in which he alleged there was widespread election fraud and corruption by the FBI under the Biden administration, and that the case was ordered directly by FBI Director Kash Patel.
Prosecutors accused Floris and Benavides of lying to Congress when they were asked about federal investigations of Hunter Biden and the veracity of information allegedly found on his laptop — but the case fell apart under scrutiny, with Judge Faruqui saying “there is simply nothing” that shows either agent intended to make false statements about the probes.
“Without motive, without direct evidence, I have nothing,” Faruqui said.
Faruqui also faulted Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche and D.C. U.S. attorney Jeanine Pirro for their public statements maligning both Floris and Benavides despite the lack of evidence, and accused the DOJ of rushing to bring charges in advance of the midterms, in apparent violation of a longstanding department practice that limits taking overt investigative steps in politically sensitive investigations within 60 days of an election.
“I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend I cannot read a calendar,” the judge said. “I will not lobotomize myself that way.”
A spokesperson for the Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Faruqui said it was the first time in his history on the bench that he had ever made a finding that the government failed to reach the relatively low burden of establishing probable cause to bring charges — which he said adds to mounting evidence that the Trump administration is unwilling to bring some of its more controversial prosecutions before grand juries.
In what he described as a “slapdash job” by the government in seeking to bring charges against decorated former agents like Floris and Benavides, Faruqui said the flawed attempt to prosecute them and the messaging by top administration officials would likely deter qualified investigators from wanting to join the FBI — and also potentially threatened Congress’ ability to get valuable testimony from future witnesses.
“This case is marketing material to discourage people from joining the FBI,” Faruqui said, before questioning “what person in their right mind” would want to join the bureau after seeing what happened to Floris and Benavides.
It’s not immediately clear whether the government will seek to appeal Faruqui’s ruling or if it will attempt to charge Floris and Benavides through other means, such as filing an amended complaint or seeking to indict them in D.C. or another district.

"I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend that I cannot read a calendar," Faruqui added.

Floris' attorney had argued in court that his client had been prosecuted in order to influence public opinion for the sake of the election.

Both Floris and Benavides had been a part of the FBI's Foreign Influence Task Force, which no longer exists but had spearheaded the agency's efforts to oppose foreign influence in the 2020 election.
The Justice Dept. has the option to pursue indictments of both Floris and Benavides through a grand jury.

A federal judge tossed a criminal complaint against two former FBI officials who falsely told Congress that evidence of Biden family criminality stemmed from a Russian disinformation campaign, decrying “weaponization.”
U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui complained that the Department of Justice had amended its criminal complaint and called the charges political given their proximity to the midterm election Tuesday, the Associated Press reported.
The Justice Department could still pursue a grand jury indictment, though it may not succeed in the liberal enclave of Washington, D.C.
“What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization,” Faruqui said, according to the AP. “I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend that I cannot read a calendar.”
Yet it appears the judge did not consult the 2020 calendar, as many of the actions that brought Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides under the scrutiny of law enforcement in the first place occurred in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election between President Donald Trump and Joe Biden.
Floris and her co-defendant Bradley Benavides have denied wrongdoing. Floris’s attorneys said in a statement last week that “the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts.”
In the lead-up to that election, the senior FBI officials muddied factual and derogatory reporting about the Biden family by labeling it part and parcel of malign Russian influence, according to the federal government’s legal complaint and declassified documents.
The team ran an FBI operation codenamed “Round River,” the aim of which was to paint derogatory information about Biden, corruption and Ukraine as Russian disinformation. The so-called “Ukraine narrative” included information about the Biden family and Burisma, Hunter Biden, Mykola Zlochevsky, and Ukraine interference in the 2016 election.
Faruqui, the federal judge, noted that the investigation was opened a day after a July primetime speech by Trump about election security.
But that speech drew on the recent discoveries of a White House Transparency Task Force helmed by journalist John Solomon.
The task force uncovered documents revealing that Floris had privately bragged about running a “shadow government” in September 2020. At the time, she was prematurely retracting a tip alleging Chinese election interference before it could be thoroughly investigated or reach Trump’s President’s Daily Brief.
“AAAAAAAH SNAPS!!!! Well done [REDACTED] THANK YOU for handling!!!” she wrote after the Albany field office that received the tip retracted it before investigating.
Floris did not stop there. As she worked to retract the explosive tip, FBI headquarters in Washington informed every field office that she would micromanage any tip alleging foreign interference.
“We’ll get this back in a box!” she informed her colleagues.
The Justice Department complaint stemmed from false statements that Floris and Benavides gave to Congress.
In August 2020, as Senate Republicans were putting their final touches on a report about Hunter Biden’s financial connections to foreign governments, Floris and other FBI officials gave them a behind-the-scenes briefing alleging their work was “a target of Russian disinformation,” per a Senate letter.
The Senate investigators — Sens. Chuck Grassley and Ron Johnson — said in the letter the FBI had not provided any evidence. They said they suspected the sole purpose of the briefing was for the unsubstantiated claim to be leaked to the media. Indeed it was eventually leaked to the Washington Post.
“Because there was no substance to the briefing … I suspected that the briefing was being given to be used at some future date for the purpose that it is now being used: to offer the biased media an opportunity to falsely accuse me of being a tool of Russia,” Johnson told the paper in response to the leak.
Other evidence indicates that Floris helped to shape the fake media narrative that the Hunter Biden laptop story was Russian disinformation.

sources.news_title: Federal Judge Dismisses Charges Against Two Former FBI Officials Accused of Lying to Congress About Hunter Biden Laptop
sources.text:
A federal magistrate judge rejected the Justice Department’s criminal case against two former FBI officials, finding insufficient evidence that they knowingly misled Congress and raising concerns about the investigation’s timing, political motivations and procedural irregularities.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WASHINGTON — A federal judge dismissed criminal charges Monday, Nov. 2, against two former senior FBI officials accused of misleading Congress about their knowledge of investigations involving Hunter Biden’s laptop, ruling that federal prosecutors failed to establish sufficient evidence of criminal wrongdoing.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui dismissed the complaint against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides following several days of contentious hearings in Washington, D.C., during which defense attorneys questioned the investigation’s origins and prosecutors faced criticism over their handling of the case.
According to Reuters’ report on the ruling, Faruqui concluded that prosecutors had not demonstrated probable cause to believe the former officials knowingly made false statements during congressional interviews in 2023.
The judge found that some statements cited by prosecutors were accurate, while others could reasonably have resulted from misunderstandings or failures of memory rather than deliberate deception.
Faruqui also questioned why the investigation had been initiated shortly after President Donald Trump publicly revisited allegations involving the 2020 presidential election and why charges were pursued immediately before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
He characterized the government’s conduct as an example of the potential weaponization of federal law enforcement, citing what he viewed as an unusually rushed investigation and procedural departures from ordinary prosecutorial practices.
The ruling represents a significant setback for the Justice Department, although prosecutors retain the option of seeking an indictment from a federal grand jury.
Floris and Benavides had been charged Oct. 23 with making false statements to Congress in connection with their previous work on the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force, which investigated potential foreign interference in American elections.
According to the Justice Department’s original charging announcement, Floris served as a deputy assistant director overseeing the task force from 2019 through mid-2022.
Benavides served as a section chief within the task force during the period preceding the 2020 presidential election.
The Justice Department alleged that both officials minimized their awareness of investigations involving Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden, when questioned by the House Judiciary Committee in 2023.
Prosecutors contended that internal communications and other evidence contradicted their congressional statements.
Floris allegedly told lawmakers that she had not participated in discussions concerning Hunter Biden while overseeing the task force.
Benavides reportedly said he first learned that the FBI possessed Hunter Biden’s laptop after reading about the matter on Wikipedia in 2023.
Federal prosecutors argued that the officials’ earlier communications demonstrated a greater degree of knowledge than they acknowledged to congressional investigators.
U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro announced the charges in October, arguing that senior law enforcement officials must be held accountable when they provide false information to Congress.
“Lying to Congress by anyone strikes at the heart of our democratic system,” Pirro said in the department’s announcement.
She maintained that FBI officials entrusted with national security responsibilities had an obligation to provide accurate information to congressional investigators.
The original complaint alleged violations of a federal statute prohibiting knowingly and willfully making materially false statements in matters within the jurisdiction of the legislative branch.
However, the case encountered immediate procedural difficulties.
During an Oct. 27 hearing, prosecutors attempted to introduce an amended criminal complaint adding an obstruction charge against both former officials.
The amended filing appeared on the court’s public docket shortly after midnight without the judicial approval ordinarily required for criminal complaints.
Faruqui rejected the filing, finding that prosecutors had bypassed procedures designed to ensure that a judge determines whether sufficient evidence exists to support criminal allegations.
According to CBS News’ account of the hearing, the judge questioned why prosecutors had departed from established procedures in a politically sensitive case.
“Everything you’re doing is making me more and more concerned,” Faruqui told prosecutors.
“Why today on this one case have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases? It makes it look like the United States is afraid of me trying to find probable cause.”
Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Borchert denied that prosecutors were attempting to avoid judicial scrutiny.
“Let me address that squarely. We are not afraid of a probable cause finding,” Borchert said.
Faruqui nevertheless ordered the amended complaint removed from the record while allowing further proceedings concerning the original false-statement allegations.
The hearings also produced testimony from FBI Special Agent Bryan Witt, who had been assigned to investigate Floris and Benavides.
Witt acknowledged under questioning by defense attorneys that the investigation began after a July speech by Trump addressing election interference and controversies surrounding the 2020 election.
He testified that FBI Director Kash Patel had directed the investigation and maintained an unusually close interest in its progress.
According to Associated Press reporting on the proceedings, Witt said he was concerned about how the investigation might be perceived.
“I had concerns that this would be political,” Witt testified.
He also described the assignment as a significant distraction from his other investigative responsibilities.
The agent’s testimony became central to the defense argument that the prosecution originated from political pressure rather than independently developed evidence of criminal wrongdoing.
Defense lawyers maintained that their clients had provided truthful responses to congressional questions based on their understanding and recollection of events that occurred several years earlier.
They also challenged the government’s interpretation of internal FBI communications, arguing that prosecutors had failed to distinguish between general knowledge of Hunter Biden-related matters and specific involvement in the investigations discussed by Congress.
Floris’ attorney, Mary Dohrmann, questioned the prosecution’s foundation and argued that the investigation reflected inappropriate political considerations.
“A political prosecution is always going to make for a shaky foundation for a criminal case,” Dohrmann said during the proceedings.
The defense further argued that the Justice Department’s decision to use a criminal complaint rather than seek a grand jury indictment was unusual given the age of the alleged offenses and the absence of an immediate public safety concern.
Criminal complaints are commonly used when prosecutors seek a prompt arrest or need to initiate proceedings before obtaining an indictment.
Federal grand juries, by contrast, determine whether sufficient evidence exists to bring formal felony charges through an indictment.
In this case, prosecutors brought the allegations through criminal complaints despite the statements under investigation having been made in 2023.
The timing attracted additional attention because the charges were announced less than two weeks before the midterm elections.
The case revived controversy surrounding the FBI’s handling of information involving Hunter Biden during the 2020 presidential campaign.
The laptop became a national political issue after reporting emerged in October 2020 concerning emails and other materials associated with Hunter Biden’s business activities.
The computer had reportedly been left at a Delaware repair shop in 2019, and copies of data purportedly obtained from it subsequently circulated among political figures and news organizations.
The FBI’s handling of the material, along with statements by former intelligence officials concerning possible foreign influence, became the subject of congressional investigations.
Republican lawmakers questioned whether federal agencies and social media companies had improperly influenced public access to information concerning the Biden family before the 2020 election.
Democrats disputed broader allegations of coordinated election interference and criticized what they viewed as politically motivated investigations.
Floris and Benavides had worked on the FBI task force responsible for examining foreign influence operations during that election cycle.
Their prosecution focused specifically on whether they knowingly misrepresented their previous involvement and knowledge when questioned by Congress.
The charges did not accuse them of stealing or altering election results.
Faruqui’s ruling addressed whether the Justice Department had presented adequate evidence to proceed with criminal false-statement charges, rather than resolving every dispute surrounding the FBI’s handling of the laptop.
According to the Washington Post’s coverage of the dismissal, the judge determined that prosecutors had not established the probable cause necessary to sustain the complaint.
Probable cause is a lower legal threshold than the proof beyond a reasonable doubt required for a criminal conviction.
The failure to satisfy that preliminary requirement prevented the prosecution from proceeding on the existing complaint.
However, dismissal at this stage does not necessarily bar the Justice Department from pursuing the allegations through another legally available procedure.
Prosecutors could attempt to present evidence to a federal grand jury and seek an indictment.
The department could also examine other available legal avenues, subject to applicable procedural requirements.
No grand jury indictment had been announced following Monday’s ruling.
The decision comes as the Trump administration faces scrutiny over several investigations involving individuals who previously held government positions or participated in inquiries connected to the president.
Trump has repeatedly criticized former federal officials over their handling of investigations involving his administration, the 2020 election and allegations concerning the Biden family.
The Justice Department has maintained that federal officials are not exempt from criminal accountability and that knowingly providing false information to Congress can constitute a serious offense.
Defense attorneys and critics of the prosecution have countered that federal criminal law must be applied without political pressure and that allegations require sufficient evidence regardless of the individuals involved.
Monday’s decision highlighted the judiciary’s role in reviewing criminal complaints before defendants can be required to answer formal charges.
It also demonstrated the significance of judicial scrutiny when prosecutors pursue cases involving politically controversial events.
Floris and Benavides remain unconvicted of the alleged offenses, and the dismissal leaves the Justice Department without an active criminal complaint against them.
Whether federal prosecutors will seek a grand jury indictment remains unresolved.
For now, the ruling marks a setback for the department’s effort to pursue criminal charges over the former FBI officials’ congressional testimony, while leaving broader questions surrounding the bureau’s handling of Hunter Biden-related investigations subject to continued political and public debate.

sources.news_title: Judge Dismisses Charges Against FBI Officials Involved With Hunter Biden Investigation
sources.text:
A federal judge on Nov. 2 threw out a criminal complaint against two former FBI officials involved in an investigation into Hunter Biden alleging they lied to Congress.
“I am deeply troubled by what has happened here in this case,” U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said in a ruling from the bench during a hearing in Washington. “What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization.”
Faruqui dismissed the case against former officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides.
“The Department disagrees with the Magistrate’s decision, which remarkably appears to suggest that high-ranking government officials are immune from accountability for making materially false statements to Congress,” a Department of Justice spokesperson told The Epoch Times in an email. “We are evaluating all options but cannot comment further on an ongoing criminal investigation. The Department’s actions will continue to be guided by the facts, the evidence, and the law—not politics.”
Lawyers for Floris said the “so-called prosecution was nothing more than a politically motivated smear campaign aimed at scoring political points before the midterm elections” and that the charges should never have been brought.
An attorney for Benavides declined to comment.
The government charged Floris and Benavides in October with lying to Congress.
Floris and Benavides were both part of the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force.
Floris said during a congressional briefing that she did not know of a Senate report on Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden, and that she was not involved with the bureau’s investigation of Hunter Biden, according to charging documents.
Benavides said during a briefing that he did not know about the FBI probe until he read Wikipedia while preparing for the briefing.
However, according to emails and other evidence prosecutors obtained, both allegedly discussed the probe, including with agents on the team investigating Hunter Biden.
And in several emails in 2020, Floris circulated the Senate report detailing financial transactions between Hunter Biden and his associates and foreigners.
Faruqui on Monday said that prosecutors did not establish that any of the statements were intentionally false or that Floris and Benavides had any motive to deceive.
“Without motive, without direct evidence, I have nothing” to go on, Faruqui said.
Faruqui also noted the investigation into Floris and Benavides was opened a day after a speech by President Donald Trump in which he brought up grievances over his 2020 election loss.
The judge also said prosecutors could have brought the case, which covers comments made in 2023, at any time, but chose just before the Nov. 3 midterm election.
“I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend that I cannot read a calendar,” Faruqui said.

sources.text:
Judge dismisses suit alleging FBI officials lied to Congress as ‘rush job’
Complaint centered on what the agents said and knew of Hunter Biden probe
A federal magistrate judge on Monday threw out a case accusing two former FBI officials of lying to Congress, criticizing it as rushed, flawed and politically motivated.
During an hourlong hearing, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia found that there was no legal justification to continue the case against Nicole Floris and Bradley Benavides.
“What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization” of government against the pair, the magistrate said, describing it as a “rush job” driven by a political push from President Donald Trump.
The government unveiled the charges last month, alleging that Floris and Benavides lied to the House Judiciary Committee during interviews in 2023 about their knowledge of a laptop that used to belong to Hunter Biden but was in possession of the FBI ahead of the 2020 election.
Faruqui, in ruling from the bench, said there was no evidence that Floris and Benavides knowingly said anything false to the committee. He also pointed to mistakes throughout the complaint against Floris and Benavides, as well as the probe that led to the charges.
“The rush to charge here led to critical mistakes,” Faruqui said.
Faruqui said he has signed off on some 400 criminal complaints in the last five years but had never held such a hearing or ruled against the government during one.
The ruling came after an unusual three-day hearing last week, which featured hours of testimony from FBI agent Bryan Witt. Witt testified that the investigation came from a direct assignment by FBI Director Kash Patel the morning after a primetime address by Trump in which he called for the prosecution of individuals involved in the agency’s shuttered Foreign Influence Task Force.
Floris and Benavides both served in supervisory positions at the task force, and Witt testified that the agency investigated the pair for months before focusing on their 2023 testimony to Congress.
Faruqui noted that the transcript showed that many of the supposedly false statements were not false and that officials did not do the work to show that Floris and Benavides knew at the time that some of their statements might have been false, a necessary element of the crime.
Statements by Judiciary Committee majority general counsel Steve Castor about the alleged lies were “inadequate, incorrect and not credible,” Faruqui said, adding that Castor talked about the impact of the supposed lies in the pair’s testimony without having attended the Benavides interview or reviewed the transcript of either interview.
According to Faruqui, the government offered an incomprehensible “word salad” justification as to why the pair might have lied to Congress by arguing they wanted to downplay the task force’s role in handling the laptop ahead of the 2020 election.
“It’s not close, it’s nothing,” Faruqui said.
The government could still appeal Faruqui’s ruling to Chief Judge James Boasberg or seek a grand jury indictment of the pair. However, Faruqui said it was “self-evident” that the government was avoiding presenting the case before a grand jury, noting he had to pause proceedings several times last week for the government to present grand jury indictments, including one failed one.
“It turns out ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days,” Faruqui said, referencing a famous aphorism that a prosecutor “could indict a ham sandwich.”
The government would have had to secure an indictment to proceed with the case regardless of his ruling. Faruqui said the decision to proceed with a complaint, coupled with the timing of the case, made him concerned about the political nature of the investigation.
“There is no other event on the calendar except for the midterm elections tomorrow,” Faruqui said. “I will not bury my head in the sand.”

Faruqui dismissed the charges without prejudice, leaving prosecutors a possible path to return while making clear that this complaint could not survive in its present form.
He pointed to the timing of the inquiry, which opened one day after President Donald Trump delivered a primetime speech revisiting allegations of 2020 election interference. An FBI agent testified that Director Kash Patel mandated the investigation and closely tracked it.
Faruqui concluded that the government’s conduct created the appearance that the criminal process had been used to satisfy political demands rather than follow evidence wherever it led.
The dismissal does not settle what happened inside the FBI in 2020. It exposes how badly a politically sensitive prosecution can collapse when investigators and prosecutors fail to follow ordinary procedure.

The Justice Department said in its original charging announcement that both defendants surrendered after arrest warrants were issued. Prosecutors alleged that each official knowingly gave materially false answers during separate House Judiciary Committee interviews in 2023 about FBI matters involving Hunter Biden.
The department identified Floris as a former supervisory special agent and Benavides as a former section chief. Both had served in leadership roles connected to foreign-influence work.
The announcement emphasized that the charges were accusations and that both defendants were presumed innocent unless proven guilty. That original account shows the government’s theory before the judge examined how the inquiry began, how the complaint was prepared and whether the investigative process could support the allegations.
Floris and Benavides denied wrongdoing, and the department acknowledged that a criminal complaint contains allegations rather than proof. The charging document was unusual because prosecutors proceeded by complaint instead of first obtaining a grand-jury indictment.
That decision put the government’s evidence and methods before a judge at an early stage—and the case began unraveling almost immediately.
During a marathon hearing, the assigned FBI agent acknowledged that some investigators viewed the inquiry as political.
Prosecutors then tried to add an obstruction charge through an amended complaint filed after midnight without first obtaining the judicial approval required for a complaint.
Faruqui rejected that filing and demanded answers about the case’s origin, timing and evidentiary foundation.

The judge’s criticism went straight to the credibility of the prosecution.
According to the ruling, the government relied on an investigation launched years after the congressional testimony and immediately after presidential pressure for charges.
Faruqui wrote that the mistakes were not harmless paperwork problems. They affected the fairness of the process and the court’s confidence that the charges were grounded in a neutral investigation.
The dismissal came without prejudice, meaning prosecutors may have a legal path to try again.
But rebuilding the case would require the Justice Department to confront the judge’s findings, repair the evidentiary record and decide whether a grand jury should hear the allegations.

A case built to expose alleged weaponization cannot itself look weaponized.
The defendants remain legally innocent of the dismissed charges, and the government has not proved that either official lied.
The Hunter Biden controversy will not disappear because this complaint failed. Congressional records, agency decisions and the bureau’s 2020 conduct remain legitimate subjects for oversight.
But criminal charges demand admissible evidence, lawful procedure and prosecutors willing to prove every element beyond a reasonable doubt.
The Justice Department had the power to bring a case with enormous political consequences.
Judge Faruqui’s ruling says it did not do the basic work required to keep that case alive.

Judge dismisses case against 2 ex-FBI officials in Hunter Biden probe
A federal magistrate judge on Monday dismissed a criminal complaint charging two former senior FBI counterintelligence officials with lying to Congress about their roles in the bureau's Hunter Biden investigation, saying the politically charged case lacked evidence and appeared to be timed with the midterm election.
In a scathing, hour-long oral ruling, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui rebuked the Justice Department and the FBI for what he called a "slapdash" case that lacked any probable cause that there was evidence Nikki Floris or Bradley Benavides had committed a crime.
"Without motive, without direct evidence, I have nothing," he said. "It's not close. It's nothing."
"I am deeply troubled by what has happened in this case," Faruqui said. "What has transpired here can't be described as anything other than weaponization."
Although the complaint was dismissed, the Justice Department could still appeal Faruqui's ruling to the chief judge or seek a grand jury indictment.
A Justice Department spokesperson said it "disagrees with the Magistrate's decision, which remarkably appears to suggest that high-ranking government officials are immune from accountability for making materially false statements to Congress."
"We are evaluating all options but cannot comment further on an ongoing criminal investigation," the spokesperson said. "The Department's actions will continue to be guided by the facts, the evidence, and the law — not politics."
CBS News has also reached out to the FBI and the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office for comment.
Floris was a former top intelligence analyst in charge at the bureau's Washington Field Office, while Benavides was the former deputy assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence Division. The two embraced outside the courtroom after the decision as Floris cried tears of relief.
They were flanked by numerous former senior Justice Department and FBI officials who had come to support them, including former Acting FBI Director Brian Driscoll and Steve Jensen, the former head of the FBI's Washington Field Office.
"This case should have never been brought," said Margaret Donovan, one of Floris' attorneys, in a statement to reporters outside the courthouse. "This was a slapdash complaint, spaghetti at the wall, Hunter Biden conspiracy fever dream. But facts still matter in a courtroom."
The criminal case against Floris and Benavides has been highly unusual since it first came to light earlier this month.
Prosecutors charged the pair in a criminal complaint, a charging document that is generally only used in felony cases that pose exigent public safety or national security threats. Usually, prosecutors secure a grand jury indictment before filing charges.
After midnight on the eve of the court hearing's first day last Tuesday, prosecutors used an unsigned and unsworn superseding complaint to try to add new charges of obstructing Congress — a maneuver the magistrate judge said was improper and unheard of.
Faruqui struck the superseding complaint from the record, saying it lacked proper judicial review. But he allowed the hearing on the original complaint to proceed in a marathon evidentiary proceeding with three days of testimony that culminated in Monday's extraordinary decision.
Throughout those three days, FBI Special Agent Bryan Witt, who was assigned to help investigate the matter, candidly acknowledged to the court that the case had not been handled like any other in his career.
He testified that it was opened at the behest of FBI Director Kash Patel just one day after President Donald Trump gave a televised speech in July where he accused intelligence officials of engaging in a coverup to hide China's interference in the 2020 election and ordered the Justice Department to pursue prosecutions. Throughout the investigation, senior officials including the FBI's deputy directors and Patel himself checked on the progress.
Witt also acknowledged that he feared it might be viewed as political and that others in his FBI field office in Kansas City were concerned it was a witch hunt.
Faruqui, a former federal prosecutor himself, at one point also quoted aloud from the Justice Department Manual, which stipulates that prosecutors should not take overt investigative or prosecutorial steps intended to affect or influence the outcome of an election.
"Why did this have to be charged in October 2026?" he asked out loud, noting there was no concern with the statute of limitations expiring in the near future.
"There was simply no other event on the calendar, except for the midterm elections," he said. He added that he refused to bury his head in the sand and pretend the timing was not an issue.
"I will not lobotomize myself in this way," he added.
The case against Floris and Benavides hinged on testimony they had provided to the House Judiciary Committee in July and September 2023.
In particular, it focused on an FBI counterintelligence operation by the Foreign Influence Task Force known as "Round River," which prosecutors said was focused on collecting "derogatory informant reporting on, among other things, Hunter Biden, to flag the reporting as Russian disinformation."
Floris served as the deputy assistant director of the FITF from mid-2019 through mid-2022, while Benavides served as its section chief from mid-2019 through the 2020 election, according to the complaint.
In those roles, Floris and Benavides provided defensive briefings to Sens. Charles Grassley and Ron Johnson in August 2020, and this ultimately led the House Judiciary Committee to summon the pair to testify about three years later.
During the three-day hearing on the case, problems with the strength of the evidence and the lack of adequate investigation came to light.
In order to show probable cause in a false statements case, prosecutors must demonstrate that the defendants made false statements, that they did so knowingly and willfully, and that those statements were material.
Faruqui ticked through each of the three elements of the offense on Monday, finding that the government had failed to meet each threshold.
He compared and contrasted the government's complaint with prior false statement cases where the elements of the offense had been met, citing the cases against former Trump national security adviser Michael Flynn and former Vice President Dick Cheney's chief of staff, Lewis "Scooter" Libby.
"It's clear to me the rushed investigation had a goal. It was a rush to charge — and that is a problem," he said.
During his testimony, Witt acknowledged, for instance, that the Republican-controlled House Judiciary Committee had refused to allow FBI agents to interview congressional staffers who had been present for Floris and Benavides' testimony — a crucial step needed to establish materiality in the case.
The only person he was ultimately allowed to speak with was Steve Castor, the general counsel for the House Judiciary Republicans, who acknowledged he had not witnessed Benavides' testimony or reviewed the transcript. Witt did not speak with anyone on behalf of the committee's Democrats.
Career prosecutors later realized the potentially fatal mistake and tried to raise it before the case was charged. In a taped conversation released to defense lawyers by the government, Carlton Davis, a political appointee who is special counsel to U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, could be heard admitting the mistake.
"I have one issue that I'm getting hammered on over here," Faruqui quoted Davis as saying. "I realize this is our f***-up."
Faruqui also noted there were numerous errors in the original charging document compared with the superseding version he later dismissed — and even Witt himself made misstatements on the stand — misstatements he noted were not criminal because he did not think Witt intended to lie.
He openly pondered why the government had failed to pressure test the case before proceeding to charge it, and likened the three-day hearing to the equivalent of an indictment review.
Instead of working out the problems and the mistakes privately within the Justice Department, he said, those issues got worked out "in open court for the whole world to watch."
He also lamented the collateral consequences that the case could have, noting it was practically "marketing material" for deterring people from joining the FBI's ranks, and would have a "chilling effect" on Congress' ability to take people's testimony. In the future, he said, Congress can expect that more people will plead the Fifth Amendment, and be deterred from appearing voluntarily as Floris and Benavides both did.
Above all, he predicted the case would erode confidence in the Justice Department and said he also felt sorry not just for the defendants, but also for the career prosecutors and agents who were forced to participate.
"This case is dismissed," he said. "I am sorry you have been dragged through this process."

The ruling by Judge Zia Faruqui followed a two-day probable cause hearing last week in the case of Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, formerly of the FBI’s now-defunct Foreign Influence Task Force.
Prosecutors claimed the duo downplayed what they knew about the bureau’s Hunter Biden probes when they sat for interviews with the House Judiciary Committee in 2023, with Benavides telling the committee he’d learned of the particulars on Wikipedia.
The Department of Justice said in a statement on X that it “disagrees with the Magistrate’s decision, which remarkably appears to suggest that high-ranking government officials are immune from accountability for making materially false statements to Congress.”

The Post broke the Hunter Biden laptop story in October 2020. Despite 51 former intelligence officials suggesting in an open letter that the report was Russian disinformation, an FBI agent confirmed the laptop was the then-first son’s at Hunter’s 2024 gun trial.
Faruqui had picked the government’s case apart, weighing each of the pair’s 10 alleged lies, with only one purported falsehood needed to survive per defendant for the case to move forward.
Floris’ legal team, led by Margaret Donovan, said in a statement Monday the case was “nothing more than a politically-motivated smear campaign aimed at scoring political points before the midterm elections” and the charges “should never have been brought in the first place.”
During the hearing, defense lawyers had taken turns grilling FBI Special Agent Bryan Witt, the government’s only witness.
Had the case moved forward, it would have been the highest-level prosecution of federal officials to come out of the laptop saga. Floris was seen weeping in the courthouse hallway during a break on the hearing’s first day, and Faruqui opened that day’s proceedings by tossing a superseding complaint prosecutors had filed after midnight.
Wednesday, the second day of the hearing, mostly belonged to Donovan, who spent the better part of the day depicting her client as an overworked bureaucrat. Donovan said Floris supervised “over 200-300 employees,” and “up to 600” after her promotion to acting assistant director. A few stray messages about Hunter Biden, she suggested, were bound to slip through the cracks.
Witt testified that agents reviewed “hundreds of thousands” of Floris’ internal communications “line by line.”
“How many hours [do you estimate she worked] in a day? Twelve, 14, 16?” Donovan asked. She argued it was unfair to “cherry-pick … five or six conversations out of hundreds of thousands.”
“You didn’t factor in the demands of her position?” Donovan chided.
“I didn’t see the relevance, no,” Witt said.
Donovan also worked through a list of what she called mitigating circumstances, including that Floris hadn’t been prepped on Hunter Biden specifically before her Judiciary Committee appearance, the events in question had occurred three years prior, and she was made to answer questions at 10 a.m., which the defense lawyer treated as roughly the crack of dawn.
“Whether it started at 10 a.m. or ended whenever … is that relevant?” Witt asked.
Much of Donovan’s cross-examination focused on semantics. Floris told the committee “I did not” when asked whether she’d been involved in the Hunter Biden investigation. Donovan also noted Floris was a counterintelligence official, not a criminal investigator, and that asking about a criminal case run by another division didn’t make her “involved” with it.

Benavides’ lawyer, Ron Safer, then made a demonstrative argument to claim the FBI officials could have misspoken, but not lied.
During redirect, prosecutors had asked Witt whether the Judiciary Committee employed Democratic staff, and Witt said he assumed so but had “no idea.” Safer pointed out that the government’s own exhibits listed Democratic staffers by title.

“I should’ve said ‘I don’t know,'” Witt said.
“But you didn’t,” Safer snapped. “Should we infer that you knowingly and willingly violated your oath?”
Donovan closed by needling Witt for consulting Steve Castor, the House Judiciary Committee’s Republican counsel, over the relevance of the alleged false statements to the committee, but not Castor’s Democratic counterpart.
“No one explained to me the partisanship nature of the committee,” said Witt, who also admitted that FBI Director Kash Patel pressed for “check-ins” on the case “weekly,” calling it the first time in his career top officials had been so involved in a false statements case.

The decision by U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui followed a dramatic hearing in which he scolded prosecutors for their unorthodox maneuvers and an FBI agent who worked the case testified that he had been concerned the investigation would be seen as “political.”
The Justice Department may still have an opportunity to pursue a grand jury indictment against the two former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, whose lawyers had pressed for dismissal of the charges. But the judge’s ruling nonetheless represents an unmistakable setback for the Justice Department, particularly given the difficulty it has had in persuading grand juries in the nation’s capital to return indictments in politically charged prosecutions like this one.
The judge’s concerns about the case were apparent almost immediately, when he raised questions about why the Justice Department had charged the case through a criminal complaint — which is more typically done when investigators have a pressing need to take a defendant into custody — as opposed to an indictment that requires a grand jury’s approval.
Then, at a preliminary hearing last week, he criticized the Justice Department for filing overnight an amended complaint with an additional criminal charge straight to the docket instead of first clearing the new charge with the court — something he said he had never seen before.
The hearing also featured testimony from an FBI agent who worked the case, who said that the investigation had been opened hours after President Donald Trump gave an election security speech last July and that it had been mandated by FBI Director Kash Patel, who kept close watch on it.
The case accused the two former FBI officials of misleading Congress in 2023 about their involvement in, and knowledge of, efforts to investigate a laptop the Justice Department says was dropped off by Hunter Biden, former President Joe Biden’s son, at a Delaware computer repair shop in 2019.
But it also sought to echo longstanding grievances by Trump and his Republican allies that the FBI attempted to suppress information during the 2020 presidential campaign that was seen as potentially harmful to the Biden family. Candidate Joe Biden, a Democrat, ultimately defeated Trump, the Republican incumbent, in the 2020 election.
The Justice Department’s case noted, for instance, how Floris and Benavides had given lawmakers in 2020 a “defensive briefing” that Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Ron Johnson of Wisconsin have said was used to undermine their investigation into the Biden administration and link it to Russian disinformation.

(CNN) — A federal judge has thrown out a case against two former FBI officials who were charged with lying to Congress as part of a winding probe from lawmakers focused in part on whether FBI investigators sought to minimize allegations of Biden family corruption and evidence related to Hunter Biden’s laptop.
The judge found there was no probable cause to bring the case.
“I am deeply troubled by what has happened in this case,” Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said during a Monday hearing announcing his dismissal of the case, adding the case was built on assumptions and began at the direction of President Donald Trump.
The case, he added, could not be seen “as anything other than weaponization,” adding that it has been “marketing material for people not to join the FBI.”
Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, both former top Washington-based intelligence specialists, were charged with one count of making a false statement.
The judge found that several of the alleged statements were not false and the ones that were lacked evidence of intent or motive to deceive.
The judge also noted how quickly the initial charges were unnecessarily rushed close to the 2026 midterm elections, adding that he “will not lobotomize myself” to that context.
Dozens of former FBI officials attended the hearing on Monday, including former Acting Director Brian Driscoll.
The case against the former FBI officials was picked apart over the course of several days last week when defense attorneys questioned an FBI agent on the case.
Faruqui noted the FBI agent testified that he found no evidence of a motive for why the former officials would lie to Congress about the laptop investigation, adding that there was no evidence that Republican lawmakers’ investigation into the Biden family slowed down or changed based on the answers the defendants provided.
“Without motive, without direct motive, I have nothing” to support a finding of probable cause, the judge said.
The political origins of the case
Defense attorneys for the two former FBI officials had scrutinized the Justice Department’s case last week, questioning one of the agents assigned to the case.
According to the FBI agent, Bryan Witt, the investigation originated after Trump, during a July primetime address, attacked officials who questioned an FBI report that China attempted to interfere in the 2020 election against Trump.
Witt testified that FBI Director Kash Patel sent a letter the following day demanding an investigation into the officials for possible conspiracy charges.
“The predication” for the case, Witt said, “was their belief that people in the intelligence community suppressed or purposely held back information that was derogatory to the Bidens.”
Inside the agency, Witt said “people generally viewed” the investigation as a “witch-hunt,” adding that he “had concerns that this would be viewed as political.”
The agent, however, never found evidence to support such a deep-state conspiracy to thwart the president and instead began scrutinizing years-old interviews the former officials had with members of Congress.
“What person in their right mind” would join the FBI after this, Faruqui questioned during Monday’s hearing.
At several moments during testimony last week, prosecutors attempted to shutdown questions over the origins of the investigation, arguing that they were only suitable for later hearings over whether the case against the former officials was selective and vindictive.
Witt testified that Patel and several top FBI officials, including deputy directors, were “routinely” updated on the case through “video conferences, in-person meetings,” emails and beyond.
The FBI leadership “were closely monitoring our progress,” Witt said, adding that such updates were unusual.
Instead of the conspiracy Patel wanted investigated, agents focused on statements the two defendants made during two meetings on the Hill, where they were asked about their knowledge of the now-infamous Hunter Biden laptop and investigations into the former president’s son.
As he was being questioned by defense attorneys, Witt repeatedly said the evidence the former officials had provided false statements was not in the complaint against them, adding he “believes we have evidence” of the alleged crime. The agent also said he had no direct evidence the two former officials intentionally misled lawmakers when answering questions about their knowledge of the laptop.
“We do not,” Witt said when asked if he had evidence Floris had motive to allegedly lie.
It was also revealed during the hearing that the staff member the FBI and prosecutors relied on to establish that Floris and Benavides’ testimony was untrue and hampered the House Judiciary committee’s investigation had not attended one of the interviews nor had reviewed the years-old transcripts.
Instead, Witt testified that a phone call with the staffer occurred on Monday, following the initial complaint against the two former FBI officials.

sources.news_title: Judge accuses DOJ of 'weaponization,' tosses case against ex-FBI officials
sources.text:
A federal magistrate judge on Monday dismissed the Justice Department’s criminal case against two former FBI officials charged in connection with the bureau’s investigations into former President Joe Biden’s son.
Bradley Benavides and Nikki Floris were charged around two weeks ago with lying to Congress in 2023 about their knowledge of the FBI’s investigations into Biden’s son, Hunter Biden. It is one of several politically charged actions by the Justice Department under President Trump in the run-up to the midterm elections on Tuesday.
At a hearing in federal court in Washington, D.C., U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui castigated the government’s investigation into Floris and Benavides, describing it as rushed and riddled with errors.
“I am deeply troubled by what has happened here,” Faruqui said in a scathing ruling from the bench. “What transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization.”
The court’s ruling came after a days-long preliminary hearing last week to determine whether probable cause existed to charge Floris and Benavides with lying to Congress. It featured testimony from one of the FBI agents who investigated the case.
In a statement, a Justice Department spokesperson said the department “disagrees with the Magistrate’s decision, which remarkably appears to suggest that high-ranking government officials are immune from accountability for making materially false statements to Congress.”
“We are evaluating all options but cannot comment further on an ongoing criminal investigation,” the spokesperson said. “The Department’s actions will continue to be guided by the facts, the evidence, and the law—not politics.”
Over the course of an hour, Faruqui on Monday laid out the basis for his decision before a packed courtroom that included many former senior FBI officials.
The judge noted that the investigation into Floris and Benavides was opened on FBI Director Kash Patel’s orders the day after President Trump delivered a primetime address on national TV in mid-July. In that speech, Trump repeated his false claims about fraud in the 2020 election and urged the FBI to investigate.
Faruqui noted that the alleged false statements were made to Congress in 2023, yet the Justice Department waited three years to pursue the case. Prosecutors then brought charges some two weeks before the midterm elections, despite a DOJ policy prohibiting timing any action to influence an election.
That was not the only unusual decision by the department. The judge also noted that charges were filed as a criminal complaint, a document usually used when there is some need for urgency such as an imminent danger, a statute of limitations deadline or a risk of flight—none of which existed in this case.
The only event that was looming here, he said, was the midterms.
“I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend I cannot read a calendar,” Faruqui said. “I will not lobotomize myself that way.”
He also said prosecutors appear not to want to take this case before a grand jury, perhaps given the Justice Department’s poor track record recently with grand juries in Washington, D.C.
On several occasions under the Trump administration, grand juries in the nation’s capital have refused to return indictments in high-profile, politically charged cases.
While Faruqui dismissed the case, he said that nothing is stopping prosecutors from going to a grand jury and trying to secure an indictment. Prosecutors could also appeal his decision to the district’s chief judge.
After the hearing, a group of former FBI officials greeted Floris and Benavides outside the courtroom. Floris, tears in her eyes, hugged several of her former colleagues before sharing a hug with Benavides.
“This case should never have been brought. The government had no case,” said Margaret Donovan, one of Floris’ attorneys. “As the judge just laid out, this was a slap-dash complaint, spaghetti-at-the wall, Hunter Biden conspiracy fever dream. But facts still matter in a courtroom. The truth still matters in a courtroom. And that’s what we say prevailed today.”

Judge Throws Out Trump’s “Slapdash” Case Reviving Hunter Biden Laptop
Judge Zia Faruqui slammed Donald Trump’s case as clear “weaponization.”
A federal judge on Monday tossed the Justice Department’s latest attempt to punish two former FBI officials who were involved in the Hunter Biden laptop investigation.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui said that the government’s case was tantamount to “weaponization,” and slammed its error-riddled arguments as “slapdash,” according to MS NOW’s Ken Dilanian.
The DOJ attempted to prosecute former intelligence analyst Nikki Floris, who ran the intelligence division at the Washington Field Office, and Bradley Benavides, a former deputy assistant director for counterintelligence. Both were charged with lying to Congress regarding Biden’s laptop contents, and surrendered on arrest warrants last month.
“This does not feel like an investigation. It feels like a broken one-wish willow obsession,” Faruqui said, comparing the case to the hit horror blockbuster Obsession.
Faruqui noted that he was “deeply troubled by what has happened here in this case,” and that the government’s procedure “cannot be described as anything other than weaponization.”
“It was a rush to charge, and that was a mistake,” Faruqui said.
The laptop scandal began in December 2019, when a Wilmington, Delaware–area computer repair shop owner gave an abandoned laptop purportedly belonging to Biden to Donald Trump’s former personal attorney Rudy Giuliani. Giuliani then handed a copy of the laptop’s hard drive to local law enforcement, which handed over the contents to the FBI.
In the years that followed, Republicans leveraged the laptop’s myriad contents to escalate scrutiny and speculation surrounding the Biden family’s business dealings with Burisma, a Ukrainian natural gas and energy company.
Giuliani and Steve Bannon, Trump’s former chief strategist, insisted that the laptop contained evidence that the Biden family made millions of dollars after former President Joe Biden and a Burisma adviser held a meeting. (The New York Post, which ran the original story on its front page, later said that the contents of the laptop were mixed with fake material and that most of the data could not be verified.)
The alleged meeting became central to an impeachment probe against the elder Biden. Republicans claimed at the time that Biden had engaged in corruption, and had peddled the influence of his vice presidency to rake in cash.
Floris and Benavides briefed Republican lawmakers in 2020 about the contents of the laptop as part of a congressional investigation. Senator Chuck Grassley has since claimed that the pair gave the briefing in order to cast the probe as Russian disinformation.
But the entire laptop investigation fell apart in 2024 after its star witness, Alexander Smirnov, admitted the conspiracy was in fact Russian disinformation. Smirnov admitted to Justice Department prosecutors that “officials associated with Russian intelligence were involved” in fabricating the Hunter Biden narrative. In the ensuing fallout, Smirnov told investigators he was in contact with “four different [top] Russian officials,” two of whom were the “heads of the entities they represent.”

A federal judge on Monday dismissed a false statements case against two former senior FBI agents accused of lying to Congress about past investigations of Hunter Biden.
In dismissing the case, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui delivered a scathing rebuke from the bench of current FBI and DOJ leadership, who he accused of seeking to impact the midterm elections.
"What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization," the judge said in tossing the case against former FBI officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides.
The dismissal follows days of testimony in a series of rare public hearings Faruqui convened to determine whether the government's case against Floris and Benavides met the low bar of probable cause.
Testimony from an FBI agent who led the case revealed it was initiated only after President Donald Trump held a July address in which he alleged there was widespread election fraud and corruption by the FBI under the Biden administration, and that the case was ordered directly by FBI Director Kash Patel.
Prosecutors accused Floris and Benavides of lying to Congress when they were asked about federal investigations of Hunter Biden and the veracity of information allegedly found on his laptop -- but the case fell apart under scrutiny, with Judge Faruqui saying "there is simply nothing" that shows either agent intended to make false statements about the probes.
"Without motive, without direct evidence, I have nothing," Faruqui said.
Faruqui also faulted Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche and D.C. U.S. attorney Jeanine Pirro for their public statements maligning both Floris and Benavides despite the lack of evidence, and accused the DOJ of rushing to bring charges in advance of the midterms, in apparent violation of a longstanding department practice that limits taking overt investigative steps in politically sensitive investigations within 60 days of an election.
"I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend I cannot read a calendar," the judge said. "I will not lobotomize myself that way."
A spokesperson for the Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Faruqui said it was the first time in his history on the bench that he had ever made a finding that the government failed to reach the relatively low burden of establishing probable cause to bring charges -- which he said adds to mounting evidence that the Trump administration is unwilling to bring some of its more controversial prosecutions before grand juries.
In what he described as a "slapdash job" by the government in seeking to bring charges against decorated former agents like Floris and Benavides, Faruqui said the flawed attempt to prosecute them and the messaging by top administration officials would likely deter qualified investigators from wanting to join the FBI -- and also potentially threatened Congress' ability to get valuable testimony from future witnesses.
"This case is marketing material to discourage people from joining the FBI," Faruqui said, before questioning "what person in their right mind" would want to join the bureau after seeing what happened to Floris and Benavides.
It's not immediately clear whether the government will seek to appeal Faruqui's ruling or if it will attempt to charge Floris and Benavides through other means, such as filing an amended complaint or seeking to indict them in D.C. or another district.
